claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates can combine wide-temperature self-lubrication with ultrahigh mechanical strength.
The initial material is a tungsten-dominated high-entropy alloy.
The tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy has high strength and ductility at ambient and elevated temperatures.
Stepwise controlled formation of coherent nanoprecipitates can strengthen the tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy.
Nanoprecipitate interfaces can function as intrinsic low-shear self-lubricating phases.
The proposed performance should be tested from room temperature to approximately 800 °C.
Room-temperature and elevated-temperature performance is relevant to aero-engine and fusion-reactor applications.
The microstructural mediator consists of coherent nanoprecipitates and their interfaces within the tungsten-based RHEA matrix.
The nanoprecipitate interfaces remain stable across the proposed temperature range.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations that could initiate premature cracking.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces create local regions of lower shear strength.
The proposed low-shear regions act as intrinsic solid-lubricating sites during sliding.
The engineered alloy will exhibit reduced friction coefficients and wear rates over a broad temperature range.
The engineered alloy will retain ultrahigh strength and ductility across the proposed temperature range.
The engineered alloy will outperform conventional tungsten-based alloys or nickel-based superalloys that lack the engineered nanoprecipitate microstructure.

Conventional high-temperature tungsten-based alloys and nickel-based superalloys generally face a trade-off between mechanical strength and lubrication or require external lubrication under extreme conditions.
The proposed benefit depends on obtaining an optimal nanoprecipitate volume fraction and spatial distribution.
Too few nanoprecipitates would provide negligible self-lubrication, whereas too many could compromise matrix continuity and degrade performance.

Direct experimental evidence connecting nanoprecipitate interfaces in tungsten RHEAs to self-lubrication is limited, and the proposed friction-reduction mechanism remains unvalidated over the full temperature range.
